title: Furniture Sales Inch Up, Rooms To Go Bets Big on Texas
subtitle: August retail data shows modest category growth, Gen Z reveals its price-first buying habits, and Rooms To Go and Rowe make the case for scale and heritage alike.

content.title: Furniture Sales Inch Up, Rooms To Go Bets Big on Texas
content.subtitle: August retail data shows modest category growth, Gen Z reveals its price-first buying habits, and Rooms To Go and Rowe make the case for scale and heritage alike.
content.greeting: Good morning. Census data confirms furniture and home furnishings sales are growing but trailing the broader retail rebound, a gap that shows up again in this week's Gen Z survey, where price and worn-out replacement drive most purchases even as three-quarters still buy sofas in-store. Rooms To Go is answering a tougher, bigger-footprint Texas market with a third new Houston-area store, while Rowe Furniture leans the opposite direction, turning an 80th anniversary into a 25-piece provenance story. Add in Legends Home's balancing act between domestic manufacturing and import sourcing, and the day adds up to a category stretching in two directions at once: volume and scarcity.

top_stories.headline: Furniture Sales Rise 1.9 Percent, Still Lagging Broader Retail
top_stories.summary: The U.S. Census Bureau's August retail report showed total sales up 6% year over year, while furniture and home furnishings store sales climbed a smaller 1.9% over August 2025 and 0.9% month over month. Retail expert Chip West attributed the gain to baseline price adjustments and back-to-college move-in demand, and furniture ranked among the weakest categories for the month alongside building materials and food and beverage stores. West expects overall retail spending to keep growing through October as retailers push holiday inventory earlier, even as shoppers lean on savings and store brands amid sticky inflation and high energy costs. Retailers should read the gap between overall retail strength and furniture's softer pace as a signal to sharpen promotions and financing offers rather than assume a broad consumer rebound will lift the category automatically.

top_stories.headline: Gen Z Shoppers Buy on Price and Replace in Three Years
top_stories.summary: Home News Now's Consumer Insights Now survey of 1,000 consumers aged 18 to 29 found most spent $500 to $999 on two furniture items this year, with sofas, primary bedroom and occasional tables leading purchases. Some 42% were replacing worn-out furniture and 24% wanted fully assembled product, while 68% researched before buying and 19% used AI in their search. Despite digital research habits, about 72% still bought sofas in-store and 71% bought recliners in-store, confirming the showroom's continued role even for a generation shopping with short-term horizons. Retailers can use this data to frame financing and warranty conversations around durability expectations that top out at five years for over a third of these buyers, not lifetime investment.

top_stories.headline: Rooms To Go Opens Conroe, Presses Texas Advantage
top_stories.summary: Top 100 retailer Rooms To Go opens a 50,000-square-foot store in Conroe on Sept. 26, its 34th Texas location and the first of three planned for the Houston market, with sites also under construction in Rosenberg, Baytown and San Marcos. CEO Jeffrey Seaman told Furniture Today the company is building larger footprints in its newer Texas stores and hopes to have eight more in development by the end of 2027. The expansion shows a Top 100 player doubling down on a competitive but growing market rather than retreating to safer territory. Independent retailers in adjacent markets should watch store design cues, since Rooms To Go treats footprint size as a merchandising tool, not just a real estate decision.

top_stories.headline: Rowe Turns 80 With a 25-Piece Gondola Reissue
top_stories.summary: Rowe Furniture will mark its 80th anniversary at High Point Market with a limited Anniversary Edition of its 1966 Gondola sofa, now commanding $7,000 to $9,000 in the vintage market, with only 25 units offered in two textile compositions and each piece signed, numbered and accompanied by a Certificate of Authenticity. President Bobby Robinson said the goal was to honor Gondola's history while keeping it distinct from surviving originals, and the sofa will not return to regular production. The move converts nostalgia and scarcity into a marketing story rather than a volume play. Retailers can borrow the tactic on a smaller scale: a numbered, limited run on a heritage item creates urgency and a press hook without disrupting core inventory.

top_stories.headline: Legends Home Balances Domestic Craft With Import Reach
top_stories.summary: A year into his role, Legends Home President David Reitz told Home News Now the company added 10 major accounts and found roughly $3 million in cost efficiencies by focusing on its strongest lines rather than chasing every opportunity. A Kaizen initiative with the Arizona Manufacturing Extension has generated an estimated $200,000 in savings, a 50% reduction in Work in Process and elimination of 4,000 operator steps. Reitz positioned Legends as one of the few remaining U.S. manufacturers able to pair domestic entertainment and mattress production with imported container business for bedroom and dining, adding investment in Vietnam and a new Asia director. The model gives retailers a hedge: a single vendor offering both quick domestic replenishment and broader import assortment reduces the number of supply relationships needed to fill a floor.

industry_moves.headline: Jensen Outdoor Leans on South American Sourcing for 2027
industry_moves.summary: President Bryan Echols told Furniture Today that Jensen Outdoor's Bolivia-based material sourcing offers proximity advantages even though it does not fully insulate the company from disruptions like local protests. Lead times remain normal, but Jensen has extended its planning horizon and is buying more inventory as a buffer. Special orders are holding up even after early buying began, and retailers are shifting more floor space to higher-end outdoor product as affluent spending stays resilient. Retailers stocking outdoor should ask vendors directly how much extra buffer inventory they are carrying this fall.

industry_moves.headline: Oriental Weavers Bets on Refresh Over Relocation
industry_moves.summary: With housing turnover slow, Oriental Weavers USA President Andy Brumlow told Home Textiles Today that rugs are positioned to capture consumers refreshing existing homes rather than moving. New collections Kate and Keenan lean into muted, layered palettes and textural, artisanal constructions, part of a broader push into washable and performance-oriented product. Brumlow said holiday will favor companies balancing design, value and dependable availability as retailers stay deliberate with inventory. Retailers can position rugs as an easy upsell for customers who are not buying full room sets this season.

industry_moves.headline: Sarreid Puts Designer Trust on the Market Agenda
industry_moves.summary: Sarreid Ltd. will host a High Point Market panel on Oct. 17 called Better Together, featuring designers Isabel Ladd, Samantha Cury and Cheryl Luckett discussing how vendor relationships translate into business results. President and CEO Brad Cates said the session is meant to be an honest look at where designer-vendor partnerships work and where they fall short. The Lunch and Learn format, paired with a showroom setting, signals how vendors are using market week to sell relationships as much as product. Retailers courting designer trade business can treat the session as a benchmark for their own account service standards.

retail_trends.headline: Amazon Raises Starting Wage as Spending Slowdown Looms
retail_trends.summary: Amazon is raising its core operations minimum starting wage to $20 per hour, pushing its average starting wage to about $24, and adding no-fee banking and grocery discount benefits for employees. The move comes as Navy Federal Credit Union's chief economist Heather Long warned a consumer spending slowdown is likely into early 2027 as gas and grocery prices squeeze middle and lower-income households. For furniture retailers, a wage hike at the country's largest employer raises the local labor cost bar and signals that big-ticket purchases will increasingly depend on financing rather than discretionary cash.

retail_trends.headline: Bread Financial Sees Consumers Guarding Cash Closely
retail_trends.summary: Mike Schmidt, macro business analyst with Bread Financial, said consumers increasingly treat cash as a precious commodity amid economic uncertainty, with tariffs and high energy prices eroding purchasing power. That caution has direct implications for big-ticket categories like furniture, where financing determines whether a sale happens at all. Retailers should revisit promotional financing waterfalls, layering primary approval, second-look options and flexible payment plans so no qualified customer walks without a path to purchase, especially as holiday season approaches.

retail_trends.headline: FabricaKraft Proves Custom Outdoor Can Scale Profitably
retail_trends.summary: Soft-furnishings brand FabricaKraft expects to hit $1 million in revenue this year, co-founder Vibhas Sen told Casual News Now, built entirely on made-to-order sizing rather than standard inventory, with a 60% to 70% conversion rate and a customer mix of roughly 75% retail and 25% B2B. The company also uses spare Sunbrella fabric scraps to build sustainability into its pitch. The model shows special orders can be a growth engine rather than a fulfillment headache when paired with clear customer education on pricing. Retailers selling custom outdoor cushions can borrow the tactic of explaining cost drivers like L-shaped cuts upfront to protect conversion.

ai_tech.headline: Claude Merges Chat and Cowork Into a Single Workspace
ai_tech.summary: Anthropic is combining Claude's chat, Cowork and Artifacts interfaces into one window so the assistant automatically routes requests instead of forcing users to pick the right tab, rolling out first to Pro and Max plans. The update also folds Claude Design into any conversation for website and prototype work. For furniture marketing and merchandising teams experimenting with AI tools, a single interface that routes tasks automatically lowers the barrier to using AI for product copy, layout mockups or catalog work without needing a dedicated specialist to manage multiple tools.

ai_tech.headline: Claude Adds Docs and Slides Built From One Conversation
ai_tech.summary: Anthropic's newly merged Claude can now generate documents and slide decks directly inside a conversation, drafting a report and matching presentation from the same request and letting users check progress from a phone before editing and downloading as PowerPoint or PDF. Senior Economist Andrew Keller described using it to pull and organize research automatically. For a furniture brand or retailer building weekly sales recaps, vendor line reviews or market-week presentations, this collapses hours of formatting work into one prompt, freeing merchandising staff to focus on the analysis rather than the deck.

ai_tech.headline: Claude Docs and Slides Roll Out to Paid Tiers First
ai_tech.summary: Superhuman's rundown confirms Claude's new Docs and Slides tools are rolling out now, starting with Pro and Max plan subscribers, with the assistant looping in the relevant tool automatically while keeping tasks and context intact in one place. The staged rollout suggests broader access, including free tiers, will follow later. Furniture retailers evaluating AI subscriptions for their marketing or merchandising teams should treat this as a low-cost pilot opportunity, testing document and presentation generation on a paid seat before committing to a wider rollout across the organization.

ai_tech.headline: ElevenLabs Brings AI Receptionists to Small Businesses
ai_tech.summary: According to Superhuman, ElevenLabs has launched an AI receptionist aimed at small businesses and freelancers, part of a wider wave of voice AI tools reaching smaller operators who lack dedicated front-desk staff. For independent furniture and mattress retailers fielding calls about store hours, delivery windows or financing questions, an AI receptionist could handle routine inquiries after hours, freeing sales staff to focus on floor traffic during business hours. The category is worth watching as pricing and furniture-specific integrations mature.

one_thing.headline: Match Your Financing Waterfall to Cautious Buyers
one_thing.body: Bread Financial's Mike Schmidt says consumers are guarding cash closely, and Census data confirms furniture sales are growing slower than retail overall. Before the holiday push, retailers should test their full financing stack, primary approval, second-look and flexible payment options, in one waterfall so a hesitant Gen Z or budget-conscious shopper always has a path to yes instead of walking out.

content.closing: Monday's Brief will track High Point Market previews, more results from the Consumer Insights Now Gen Z series, and any fresh signals from the September retail data as the holiday buying window opens.
